html:
A report is only as good as the decision it feeds. When a stakeholder can say exactly which decision the report informs, the report becomes evidence; without that, it is decoration. This phase teaches you to turn business questions into report requirements, choose report types and filters that return trustworthy datasets, pick the chart that matches the decision, and assemble dashboards whose every component drills into a detail report. BrightLogistics' lead-rollout and the Business_Analyst permission set in the repo give you a live lab for every concept.

Learning Objectives

  • Turn a stakeholder question into a report requirement that names question, audience, object, grouping, and filter...
  • Select and design a report type with the correct primary object and related objects...
  • Apply filters and filter logic, including custom logic for A AND (B OR C)...
  • Choose the right chart for the decision a component must drive...
  • Build a dashboard as a decision cockpit whose components drill into detail reports...
  • Define KPIs with targets, owners, and a "what will you do" answer...
  • Reference the repository's one dashboard, two reports, and Business_Analyst license evidence...
  • Validate report output with the stakeholders who will act on it...

1. From Business Question to Report Requirement

Start with the decision, not the data. A report requirement names the QUESTION, the AUDIENCE, the OBJECT, the GROUPING, and the FILTER. If a stakeholder cannot state the decision they will act on, the report is decoration, however pretty.

QuestionReportGroup by / filter
Which sources convert best?Opportunities wonSource -> Close Won
Is UAT on track?UAT test casesStatus summary by story
Which requirements are unsized?User storiesWHERE Story_Points__c = null
Adoption OK?LoginsWeekly active users

The question-and-decision pair is the test. "Which sources convert best?" implies a decision: shift lead-gen budget toward the converting sources. "Is UAT on track?" implies the decision to extend, gate, or ship. Write the pair at the top of the requirement and the rest of the build flows from it.

The standard requirement template used in this academy sits in ReportRequirementService (section 11) and reads like a data object:

md
KPI: "Average requirement-to-story coverage by sprint"
Source report: Requirements Summary (grouped by Sprint__c)
Component: bar chart, limit 10 bars, color by Status__c
Audience: Delivery Lead - sees it daily

Audience matters as much as question: an executive needs the answer in one screen; an operations lead needs the drill-down. Capture audience at the start and you will not overbuild.

2. Anatomy of a Report: Report Type

The report type defines which objects participate (primary + related) and which records may appear. The primary object is what you are counting: it decides the unit of every row. Related objects join for context.

  • Standard report types cover Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Opportunities, Cases, Tasks, and platform basics.
  • Custom report types exist because a custom object like UAT_Test_Case__c or User_Story__c has no standard type until you create one, usually through a lookup relationship (Lead with User_Story, Story with UAT_Test_Case).

Choose the primary object by the question: counting test cases grouped by story means the primary object is UAT_Test_Case__c with a lookup to User_Story__c as context. Counting stories that have test cases reverses it. The rule: primary = what you count; related = what you add for meaning. Mis-set the primary and every total is subtly wrong, and no dashboard filter can fix it.

3. Report Types in Practice

For BrightLogistics and the repo's teaching org, the recurring types are:

QuestionPrimary objectRelated objectsRecords included
Requirements by statusBusiness_Requirement__cUser_Story__c (lookup)All with a Type
Story backlog healthUser_Story__cUAT_Test_Case__cStatus != Won't Have
UAT progressUAT_Test_Case__cUser_Story__cType = Test Case
Adoption / loginsLogin History (standard)UserAll logins in window

The repo ships two reference reports under force-app/main/default/reports/ — study their XML: which object, which fields, which filter, which format. Building your own version in the Report Builder and re-creating the dashboard (force-app/main/default/dashboards/) is the phase's hands-on path, because the reference metadata is a simplification designed to be rebuilt by hand.

4. Filters and Filter Logic

Filters tighten the dataset; grouping rolls it up. Every filter is "field op value", and filters combine with AND/OR. When the stakeholder's request is more than a flat AND, Salesforce supports custom filter logic — (1 AND 2) OR 3 style syntax that references each filter by its position.

A real default-set example in the report-type selection is the OR within an AND: you want stories whose Status is Done AND (Priority is Must Have OR Source is Web). In the builder you create filter 1 (Status = Done), filter 2 (Priority = Must Have), filter 3 (Source = Web), then set custom logic to 1 AND (2 OR 3). The parentheses matter: 1 AND 2 OR 3 is a different dataset and will silently include stories you never wanted.

Two habits keep filters honest: (a) validate the count before and after each filter is added, so a filter that zeroes the report is caught immediately; (b) remember dashboard filters hide rows, they do not fix a wrong report type — always validate the underlying report first. When someone complains "the number is wrong", debug the report, not the dashboard.

5. Summary and Matrix Reports

Reports come in formats that do different jobs:

  • Tabular — a straight list of rows, no grouping; good for exports and detail lists.
  • Summary — groups by a field (e.g., Status) and totals per group; the workhorse for KPIs ("count of UAT cases by status").
  • Matrix — groups by two dimensions (rows and columns), grid style; good for cross-tabs like "status by sprint".

Each dashboard source component in this roadmap is a summary or matrix report because components total and chart at the group level. Build the summary first — "requirements summary grouped by Sprint__c" — then let the dashboard slice it. A related-note: join-back totals from the primary object are what a count column displays, so totals must match the report type's row semantics or the dashboard shows a number nobody can reproduce.

6. Choosing the Right Chart for the Decision

The chart is a decision aid, so pick the chart that matches the decision the component drives:

DecisionChartNote
Where is the pipeline?Funnel / DonutGreat for stage distribution
Is a KPI on target?GaugeOne number against a threshold
Trend over time?Line (or multi-axis)Time series, two axes
Distribution across groups?Bar / stacked barCompare categories or composition
Relationship?ScatterTwo numeric fields

Ask the leadership question first: "what will you DO when the gauge turns red?" If the answer is nothing, replace the gauge. BrightLogistics' Adoption Dashboard chooses a funnel for pipeline stage, a stacked bar for requirement health, a gauge for UAT sign-off, and a multi-axis line for adoption trend (section 8) — every chart maps to a decision and a next action.

7. Dashboards: The Decision Cockpit

A dashboard is a decision cockpit: 5-8 components on one screen, aimed at one owner audience, and every component must drill into a detail report. The rules of the cockpit:

  • One screen — if it needs scrolling through three tabs, split the dashboard.
  • One audience — executive enrollment is not operations UAT; do not mix.
  • Every component drills down — the decision a gauge signals must lead to the report that shows the records behind it.
  • Color and thresholds are set by agreed KPI targets, not aesthetic taste.
ComponentChartDrill-down
Pipeline by StageFunnel / DonutOpportunity list report
Requirements healthStacked barRequirements summary
UAT sign-offGaugeUAT test case report
Adoption trendLine multi-axisLogin history

The drill-down rule is what makes dashboards actionable: the viewer turns "UAT is red" into "here are the failing test cases" in one click. A dashboard without drill-downs is a poster.

8. KPIs That Drive Action

A KPI is a number with a target, an owner, and an action. The difference between a metric and a KPI is purpose: a KPI is tied to a goal the business agrees to move. BrightLogistics' project KPIs from the brief make ready examples:

KPITargetOwnerAction when off the target
Lead-to-dispatch cycleUnder 4 hours (from ~48h)Ops LeadEscalate blockers in the queue
Auto-assignment ratioAt least 80% of inbound leads without re-entryDelivery LeadFix assignment rules
Requirement-to-story coverage100% of approved requirements tracedBAChase untraced stories
UAT sign-off rate100% before go-live gateBA / PMStop, fix, re-test

Every KPI you name should pass the "what will you do" test, and the dashboard gauge sits on the KPI with the action documented next to it — ideally as a Task or in the adoption report's notes. The repo's certification custom metadata and ChangeManagementService carry adoption targets; reuse those goals when you build the executive view.

9. The Repository's Reports and Dashboard

The lab org ships one dashboard and two reports under force-app/main/default/:

  • Two reports (in force-app/main/default/reports/) exercising the report-type + summary + filter patterns above.
  • One dashboard (in force-app/main/default/dashboards/) composing them into a cockpit with drill-downs.
  • The Business_Analyst permission set (force-app/main/default/permissionsets/Business_Analyst.permissionset-meta.xml) granting access to reports folders, dashboards, and the app — this is the "right people see the evidence" half of analytics credibility.

Deploy them to the lab (or the auto-scala path in README), open the dashboard, and trace each component to its source report, then to the folder security granted by the permission set. Rebuild them by hand in the UI once — that exercise is the fastest way to internalize report type vs. filter vs. format, and it is exactly what the reference-metadata note in the README encourages.

10. Validating Report Output with Stakeholders

A report that nobody can reproduce is a report nobody trusts. Validation has three layers:

  1. Sanity the numbers — cross-check a small known dataset by hand: create two stories, run the report, and confirm the count.
  2. Sanity the filters — recompute the filter logic against the record set you know you inserted, and test the custom-logic parentheses.
  3. Sanity the decision — replay the dashboard with the stakeholder: "here is the gauge, here is the drill-down, would this change what you do Monday?"

Run validation with the owners BEFORE the dashboard goes live, because the expensive failure is the executive who trusts a number once and never trusts it again. Annotate date-ranges and filter definitions on the dashboard (via the component titles) so the same report next quarter is read the same way today.

11. The ReportRequirementService Pattern

ReportRequirementService (force-app/main/default/classes/ReportRequirementService.cls) turns a KPI into a report requirement object — the data-model for the template in section 1. Study it as the structured answer to "how do BAs capture analytics ask". Its fields mirror the requirement skeleton: the question, the audience, the primary object, the grouping, the filter, the component type, and the drill-down report.

Read the service, then practice writing report requirements for the six-question backlog in section 1 before opening any builder. When the builder opens, you are executing a spec, not designing on the fly — which is exactly the BA discipline Phase 9 taught for automation and this phase teaches for analytics.

12. Common Pitfalls and BA Tips

  • Building before the question — a report without a decision is decoration; capture question + audience first.
  • Wrong primary object — totals are silently wrong; the unit of the row is set by the primary object.
  • Flat AND-only filters — meetings ship the wrong dataset; use custom filter logic with tested parentheses.
  • Dashboard filters as a fix — dashboard filters hide rows, they cannot fix a wrong report type; validate the report first.
  • Component soup — more than 5-8 components, or mixed audiences, and the cockpit becomes noise.
  • No drill-downs — a header that shows red but cannot reach its records is a poster.
  • Evergreen KPIs — a target nobody owns is a wish; give every KPI an owner and an action.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Write Report Requirements for the Six Questions

Steps:

  1. Copy the six questions from section 1 into a table, then for each write question, decision, audience, primary object, grouping, and filter.
  2. For the two tricky ones (UAT progress; requirements unsized), add the custom filter logic expression in 1 AND (2 OR 3) style.
  3. Compare with the ReportRequirementService shape and adjust.

Expected result: six complete report requirements, each with a decision and a testable filter. What it proves: the requirement template precedes and prevents bad builds. (Your six-requirement set is the feedstock for exercise 10.1 in Phase 15.)

Exercise 10.2 — Rebuild the Two Reports from the Reference Metadata

Steps:

  1. Deploy force-app/main/default/reports/ to the lab and study the XML for both reports (object, fields, filter, format).
  2. Recreate each report from scratch in the Report Builder and compare counts with the deployed version.
  3. Insert two known test records and confirm the filter logic includes and excludes exactly the right rows.

Expected result: two rebuilt reports whose every number reproduces the reference metadata. What it proves: report types and filter logic are readable, buildable, and verifiable artifacts. (The same two-reference are exercised in 10.2 of Phase 15.)

Exercise 10.3 — Build a KPI Dashboard from Scratch

Steps:

  1. From your six requirements, choose 3-4 components for one BrightLogistics audience (e.g., Delivery Lead).
  2. Create a dashboard, add each component from a summary report, set each component's drill-down to its detail report.
  3. Assign the Business_Analyst permission set and verify a reviewer with it can open the dashboard and drill down.

Expected result: a 3-4 component dashboard, every component drilling to its report, secured by the permission set. What it proves: dashboards are decision cockpits with owners, targets, and drill-downs — not charts pasted together. (Deepen with the adoption-dashboard variant in exercise 10.3 of Phase 15.)

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
Report requirementThe object-shaped spec: question, decision, audience, object, grouping, filter.
Report typeThe definition of primary + related objects and which records the report can show.
Primary objectThe object being counted; sets the unit of every row.
Filter logicAND/OR bracketing (1 AND (2 OR 3)) controlling how filters combine.
Summary reportA report that groups rows and totals at the group level.
Matrix reportA report grouping by two dimensions into a grid.
DashboardA collection of chart components on one screen, each drilling into a detail report.
Drill-downThe navigation from a dashboard component to the report behind its data.
KPIA metric with a target, an owner, and an agreed action.
Custom report typeA report type built for a custom object via its lookup relationships.
Business_Analyst permission setThe repo's access bundle granting report/dashboard/app visibility.

Certification Checkpoints

  • Convert a stakeholder question into a complete report requirement...
  • Choose the primary object for a custom report type and justify it...
  • Build filters with custom logic and test the parentheses against known data...
  • Pick the chart that serves the decision a component must drive...
  • Design a dashboard where every component drills down into a detail report...
  • Define a KPI with target, owner, and the "what will you do when it fails" answer...
  • Reference the repo's one dashboard and two reports in force-app and the Business_Analyst permission set...
  • Validate report output with stakeholders before go-live...

Summary

You can now turn vague asks into report requirements, pick the right primary object and filter logic, choose the chart that serves the decision, and assemble dashboards whose components drill into evidence — all anchored by KPIs that carry owners and actions. You know the repository's one dashboard and two reports, and why the Business_Analyst permission set is the trust layer under every number. You have completed the roadmap's analysis core: stories, ceremonies, wireframes, automation, and now the reports that prove the system works. The next phases build on it with gap analysis, UAT, and the change management that makes these dashboards actually move the business.
